definition: Two completely separate, unrelated attach mechanisms exist in the standard Roblox weapon pipeline and do not automatically sync: (1) a `WeldConstraint` (`Part0`/`Part1` set to the rig's hand and the tool mesh) added directly under a Rig Builder dummy purely so the tool is VISIBLE while posing in the Animation Editor — this weld is never exported, never referenced again, and has no bearing on the shipped game; and (2) the actual `Tool`'s own `Grip` property (a CFrame with position and orientation sub-properties) which is the ONLY thing that determines how the tool is actually held in a real player's hand at runtime, configured completely independently, later, on the entirely separate `Tool` instance the animation gets published to play on.
purpose: Let an animator see a held prop in roughly the right place while posing an animation (system 1), without that preview setup having any relationship to, or substituting for, correctly configuring how the item is actually gripped at runtime (system 2) — these solve two different problems and this source does not treat them as connected.
visible_effect: The animator's own preview during posing can look reasonable (weld-based, position approximate) while the FIRST live playtest of the actual equipped tool shows a visibly wrong grip (rotated/offset incorrectly) — because nothing carried the preview weld's positioning over to the Tool's Grip property; they were never the same data.
psychological_or_gameplay_effect: A specific, demonstrated confusion/surprise ('you'll notice that my sword grip is a little wonky') from a presenter who had just finished a careful authoring-time weld setup and reasonably but incorrectly expected it to already be reflected in the runtime result.
physical_interpretation: None — two independent pieces of transform data (a temporary authoring-scene weld's implicit offset vs. the Tool's own persistent Grip CFrame) with no code or tool in this pipeline that derives one from the other.
use_cases: any Roblox weapon/tool pipeline using the Rig Builder + Animation Editor to author a held-item animation before separately configuring a real `Tool`'s Grip for gameplay
understanding why a carefully-posed authoring-time preview does not guarantee a correct runtime hand grip, and budgeting separate trial-and-error time for the Grip step specifically
non_use_cases: a pipeline where the SAME instance is used for both authoring preview and runtime (not what this source demonstrates, but would eliminate this exact gap if it existed)

an item with no Grip concept at all (e.g. a prop attached purely within an animator for offline rendering, never equipped as a Roblox `Tool`) — see `easyweld_join_in_place_preserves_relative_transform`, W08-71, for that different case
interactions: weapon_attach_under_root_avoids_subframe_chain_desync (W05-43) — that entry's still-open cadence_representation question (does `attach_item` preserve a hand-placed offset, or reset it?) is now sharpened by direct evidence: in the REAL Roblox pipeline this source demonstrates, the answer is genuinely 'neither system talks to the other' — a caller cannot assume an in-animator attach offset survives into a runtime Grip without a SEPARATE, explicit step

easyweld_join_in_place_preserves_relative_transform, tool_handle_cancollide_massless_grip_editor_construction (W08-71, W08-77, this batch) — this entry names the SAME underlying two-systems gap from a third angle: Moon Animator's EasyWeld and the Tool Grip Editor are ALSO two separate mechanisms (an authoring-time weld and a runtime Grip editor plugin) that happen to be easier to keep in sync because the Grip Editor plugin visually previews the live Grip result directly, unlike this video's manual CFrame-property guessing approach
cadence_representation: This is the most direct evidence yet for the open question already flagged in `weapon_attach_under_root_avoids_subframe_chain_desync`'s `cadence_representation`: whether `attach_item`'s offset is preserved into whatever a real Roblox `Tool`'s Grip ends up being after `export_to_studio`. This source shows that in the vanilla Roblox pipeline, an authoring-time attach and a runtime Grip are simply two unrelated pieces of data unless a tool deliberately derives one from the other — Cadence's own `attach_item` offset is exactly the kind of EXACT, COMPUTED data (this build's own standing constraint: exact, not estimated) that COULD be carried through into a correct Grip CFrame automatically, which would be a genuine improvement over this entire video's manual trial-and-error process. Not confirmed either way in this session — a future session should check whether `export_to_studio`/the bridge does this derivation today.
control_surface: `attach_item`'s offset and `export_to_studio`'s output are the relevant surfaces; whether the latter derives a Roblox Grip from the former was not verified in this session.
detection_and_measurement_methods: Not a motion measurement — a pipeline/data-flow question, checkable by reading `export_to_studio`'s implementation and the bridge's `buildAnimation` handler directly.
generation_or_modification_methods: Not implemented in this build; if not already done, deriving a Grip CFrame from `attach_item`'s own exact, computed offset would eliminate exactly the manual guess-and-check process this video's whole final section consists of.
failure_modes: the source's own extended, explicit trial-and-error: guessing the wrong rotation axis, then the wrong sign, then the wrong position axis, then the wrong sign again — 'once again we somehow got it wrong for a third time in a row' — four to five full playtest cycles to find a correct Grip CFrame purely by guessing, with no computed guidance available at any point
assuming an authoring-time weld's visual placement is 'the answer' the runtime Grip should match, when nothing in this pipeline actually transfers that information
roblox_considerations: Entirely native Roblox concepts: `WeldConstraint` (Part0/Part1) for the authoring-time preview, and `Tool.Grip` (a CFrame, exposed in Studio as separate Position/Orientation sub-properties) for the runtime hand attachment — two different instance types serving two different moments in the pipeline, with no engine-level link between them.
performance_implications: None — both are one-time authoring/configuration steps.
examples: a `WeldConstraint` added under a Rig Builder dummy with Part0=RightHand, Part1=the sword mesh, purely so the sword is visible while animating in the Animation Editor (video @ 00:47–02:00)

the SEPARATE, later, real `Tool`'s Grip orientation/position properties adjusted by pure trial-and-error across five playtest cycles — wrong Y-axis rotation, wrong X-axis sign, wrong position axis, wrong sign again, before landing on a correct grip (video @ 08:38–10:50, confirmed in this session's own frame at t=10:39 showing an in-progress playtest with the sword visibly mispositioned)
evidence_status: video: https://youtu.be/nKC3-pAtN5g @ 00:47–10:50 — Rustysillyband (the presenter) demonstrates both systems directly, including the explicit surprise at the mismatch and the full guess-and-check Grip-tuning process; UI/result confirmed in this session's own frames at t=08:37 (LocalScript with animation id) and t=10:39 (mid-trial-and-error playtest); experimental until validated
